hints: Look closely at the phrase 'bound by a single membrane' and list which organelles this means, like RER, Golgi apparatus and secretory vesicles, not mitochondria or nuclei.
Ask yourself which of these four cells is a specialist secretory cell that must package and export large amounts of mucus using RER, Golgi and vesicles.
walkthrough:
**Recall what single membrane means**

Great start, let us sort our organelles. Single membrane structures include rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, vacuoles, lysosomes and secretory vesicles.

Remember, mitochondria, chloroplasts and the nucleus are double membrane, while ribosomes, centrioles and cilia are not membrane bound at all.

**Link structure to cell job**

Now think function. A cell that secretes a lot of protein, like mucus or enzymes, will need huge amounts of RER to make it, Golgi to modify and package it, and vesicles to carry it. That means lots of single membrane volume.

**Compare the four cells and decide**

A goblet cell is a specialist mucus-secreting cell, so its cytoplasm is packed full of RER, Golgi and mucus vesicles. The other cells rely more on double membrane mitochondria, non-membrane structures, or have almost no organelles, so B has the highest proportion.

options.A: Ciliated cells need many mitochondria (double membrane) for ATP and centriole-like basal bodies (no membrane) for cilia, so single membrane structures are not dominant.
options.B: Goblet cells secrete mucus, so they are filled with extensive RER, Golgi apparatus and secretory vesicles, all single membrane bound.
options.C: Mature mammalian red blood cells lose their nucleus and most organelles to make room for haemoglobin, so they have almost no single membrane structures.
options.D: Companion cells are metabolically very active for loading phloem, so they are rich in mitochondria (double membrane) and ribosomes rather than secretory membranes.
